name: UX / UI Design
tagline: Portfolio decides everything — which cuts both ways.
description: UX and UI designers decide how software works and how it looks: research what users need, structure the flow, design the screens, test whether people can actually use it. No degree is required anywhere in this field — hiring is portfolio-driven almost exclusively. The honest counterweight is that the junior design market is crowded and tightened significantly after 2022, so the portfolio bar is genuinely high.

salaryRange.note: Junior UX/UI designer range in US markets; freelance rates vary enormously ($25–75/hr starting). Mid-level designers commonly reach $85K–120K. Product designers at tech companies earn more; agency and in-house non-tech roles pay less.

remoteFriendly.note: Design collaborates in Figma, which is built for remote work. Junior designers are more often asked to be in-office or hybrid because critique and mentorship happen faster in person.

realityCheck: Three-screen 'redesigns' of famous apps do not get people hired anymore — everyone has them. What works is 2–3 deep case studies showing research, iteration, failed attempts, and measurable outcomes. Expect the portfolio to take four to six months on its own, and expect freelance or volunteer work to be part of getting the first salaried role.
whyItFits: Retail work is a long education in watching people fail to find things, misread signs, and give up at checkout. That's usability research done in person for years. Designers who genuinely understand frustrated non-technical users are rarer than designers who can make a screen look nice.

motivation.quote: Nobody in this field will ask where you studied. They will ask to see your work, and then they will ask why you made each decision.
motivation.story: Designers reach this field from graphic design, teaching, retail, customer service, and nursing — the common thread is a portfolio with genuine reasoning in it. The people who struggle are the ones who treat the portfolio as a gallery of pretty screens. The ones who get hired write case studies that read like investigations: here was the problem, here's what users told me, here's what I tried, here's what failed, here's what shipped.
motivation.source: Composite of the pattern described in r/UXDesign and Nielsen Norman Group career articles

interviewPrep.question: Walk me through one project from your portfolio.
interviewPrep.why: The entire interview usually hangs on this. Structure: the problem, who the users were, what research you did, what you learned that surprised you, what you designed, what testing showed, what you changed, and what you'd do differently with more time.

interviewPrep.question: How do you know your design is good?
interviewPrep.why: Answer with evidence, not taste: usability testing, task completion rates, error rates, support ticket volume, conversion. A designer who answers 'it looks clean' fails this question.

interviewPrep.question: What's the difference between UX and UI?
interviewPrep.why: UX: how it works, structure, flow, whether it solves the problem. UI: the visual and interactive layer. Note that most jobs need both and the split is more academic than practical.

interviewPrep.question: An engineer says your design can't be built in the time available. What now?
interviewPrep.why: They're testing collaboration. Ask what's expensive, find where the value actually is, propose a simpler version that preserves the core, involve engineering earlier next time.

interviewPrep.question: How do you make a design accessible?
interviewPrep.why: Color contrast ratios (WCAG AA is 4.5:1 for body text), keyboard navigation, semantic structure and screen reader support, not relying on color alone, hit-target sizing. Accessibility questions are increasingly common and are a fast way to stand out.

interviewPrep.question: Tell me about feedback that changed your design.
interviewPrep.why: They're checking ego. Have a real example where you were wrong and the work got better.

interviewPrep.question: How does your design work connect to business goals?
interviewPrep.why: The question that separates junior from mid-level. Tie design decisions to retention, conversion, support cost, or task completion — not to aesthetics.

steps.title: Learn UX fundamentals and the design process
steps.description: User research, personas and jobs-to-be-done, information architecture, wireframing, prototyping, usability testing, and iteration. Start with theory from the field's primary sources rather than from social media designers — the free Nielsen Norman Group and Laws of UX material is better than most paid courses.
steps.costNote: Free. The best foundational UX writing in the field is published free.
steps.outcome: You can describe and defend a design process end to end.

resources.name: Nielsen Norman Group — free articles and videos
resources.notes: Free. The most authoritative free UX research library that exists. Their paid courses are expensive and unnecessary at this stage.

resources.name: Laws of UX
resources.notes: Free. Short, memorable principles with the research behind them.

resources.name: Google UX Design Professional Certificate (Coursera)
resources.notes: PAID: $49/month, roughly $200–300 total. Good structure and produces three portfolio pieces — but everyone else has the same three, so treat them as practice rather than as your portfolio. Financial aid available.

resources.name: Interaction Design Foundation
resources.notes: PAID: roughly $16–20/month annual membership. Deep course library; optional.

steps.title: Master Figma
steps.description: Figma is the industry standard and its free tier is genuinely sufficient for learning and for a portfolio. Learn frames, auto layout, components and variants, constraints, prototyping, and design systems. Auto layout in particular is the skill that separates people who can produce professional files from people who can't.
steps.costNote: Free. Figma's free Starter plan allows unlimited personal files and is what most learners use. Paid plans are for team collaboration features you don't need yet.
steps.outcome: You can build a responsive, component-based prototype in Figma without fighting the tool.
steps.resumeBullet: Advanced Figma proficiency: auto layout, component libraries and variants, interactive prototyping, and maintainable design systems.

resources.name: Figma (free Starter plan)
resources.notes: Free. Runs in a browser, which means it works on a library computer — though a mouse and a real screen make it much less painful.

resources.name: Figma Learn — official free tutorials
resources.notes: Free official training.

resources.name: Figma Community files
resources.notes: Free. Open other designers' files and study how professionals structure their work — an unusually direct way to learn craft.

steps.title: Learn visual design fundamentals
steps.description: Typography, spacing and rhythm, color theory and contrast, hierarchy, grids, and layout. This is the part self-taught designers most often skip and it's the most visible gap in a weak portfolio. Study interfaces you admire and reproduce them precisely to understand the decisions inside them.
steps.resumeBullet: Applied visual design fundamentals — typography, spacing systems, color and contrast, and hierarchy — to produce accessible, consistent interfaces.

resources.name: Refactoring UI (article series and free tips)
resources.notes: Free article series; the book is paid (~$99) and optional. Extremely practical for non-designers.

resources.name: Practical Typography (free online book)
resources.notes: Free to read. Opinionated and correct.

resources.name: Material Design and Apple Human Interface Guidelines
resources.notes: Free. Real design systems maintained by the companies that ship at the largest scale.

resources.name: WebAIM contrast checker
resources.notes: Free. Check every color pair you use — accessibility failures are the fastest way to lose credibility in a portfolio review.

steps.title: Do real user research
steps.description: Interview five real people about a real problem. Watch them use an existing product and take notes on where they hesitate, guess, or give up. This step is what makes a case study credible — a portfolio piece with actual research in it beats a visually prettier one without, in almost every review.
steps.costNote: Free. Recruit from people you know; use free tools for notes and recordings (with permission).
steps.outcome: Research findings from real humans that changed what you designed.
steps.resumeBullet: Conducted user interviews and moderated usability tests, synthesizing findings into design decisions and measurable interface improvements.

resources.name: NN/g — user interview and usability testing guides
resources.notes: Free methodological guidance from the people who defined the methods.

resources.name: Maze / Useberry free tiers (unmoderated testing)
resources.notes: Free tiers available for remote unmoderated usability testing.

steps.title: Build 2–3 deep portfolio case studies
steps.description: This is the path. Not screens — case studies: the problem, who it affects, the research, the alternatives you considered and rejected, the tests, what failed, what you changed, and what the outcome was. Solve real problems for real people (a local business, a nonprofit, a friend's side project) rather than redesigning Spotify. Real constraints produce better stories.
steps.costNote: Free. Portfolio hosting is free on Notion, Framer's free tier, or GitHub Pages. A custom domain (~$12/year) is worth it once the work is good.
steps.outcome: A portfolio site with 2–3 case studies that show reasoning, not just screens.
steps.resumeBullet: Designed and shipped end-to-end product experiences documented as case studies: user research, information architecture, wireframes, high-fidelity prototypes, usability testing, and measured outcomes.

resources.name: Case study structure guides (NN/g and Bestfolios examples)
resources.notes: Free examples of what strong junior case studies look like. Study structure, don't copy content.

resources.name: Notion (free portfolio hosting)
resources.notes: Free personal plan with public page publishing. Plenty of hired designers use a Notion portfolio.

resources.name: Framer free tier
resources.notes: Free tier with a framer.website subdomain. A designed portfolio site is itself a work sample.

steps.title: Learn design-to-development handoff
steps.description: Understand what happens after you hand off: how developers consume your files, why component-based design matters, what design tokens are, and enough HTML and CSS to know when you're asking for something expensive. Designers who can talk to engineers are meaningfully more hireable than those who can't.
steps.outcome: You can hand a developer a file they don't have to ask questions about.
steps.resumeBullet: Prepared production-ready design handoffs: component specifications, design tokens, responsive behavior documentation, and accessibility annotations.

resources.name: freeCodeCamp — Responsive Web Design certification
resources.notes: Free. Enough HTML/CSS to understand what you're asking developers to build.

resources.name: Figma Dev Mode documentation
resources.notes: Free documentation on how developers consume Figma files.

steps.title: Take on freelance or volunteer client work
steps.description: Real clients with real constraints produce the portfolio pieces that get people hired, and they also produce references. Start with nonprofits and small local businesses — a landscaping company's booking flow is a better case study than another Spotify redesign, because it has a real user, a real constraint, and a real outcome.
steps.costNote: Free — and it should pay you at least something once you've done one or two. Do not pay to join a 'design internship' program.
steps.outcome: Client work, references, and case studies with real outcomes.
steps.resumeBullet: Delivered UX/UI design for small business and nonprofit clients: requirements gathering, prototyping, usability testing, and developer handoff.

resources.name: Catchafire (nonprofit skills-based volunteering)
resources.notes: Free. Nonprofits post design projects; scoped work with a real client and a reference at the end.

resources.name: Upwork / Contra (freelance platforms)
resources.notes: Free to join; platforms take a commission. Rates start low — treat early jobs as portfolio acquisition rather than income.

resources.name: ADPList (free mentorship from working designers)
resources.notes: Free 1:1 portfolio reviews with working designers. One of the highest-value free resources in the field — book a review before you start applying.

steps.title: Get portfolio reviews, then apply
steps.description: Before applying, get your portfolio critiqued by working designers — free mentorship platforms exist specifically for this, and the feedback will be blunt and useful. Then apply broadly, including to in-house roles at non-tech companies (banks, insurers, healthcare, universities), where the competition is far lighter than at product startups.

resources.name: ADPList — free portfolio reviews
resources.notes: Free mentorship sessions with designers at real companies.

resources.name: r/UXDesign portfolio feedback threads
resources.notes: Free and unsparing. Read the sidebar and the recurring portfolio threads before posting.

resources.name: Indeed / LinkedIn — junior UX designer listings
resources.notes: Free. Also search 'product designer', 'UI designer', 'digital designer', and 'web designer' — the titles are used inconsistently.
